{{Short description|Polynesian language}} {{use dmy dates|date=July 2024}} {{Infobox language |name=Tikopia |states=[[Solomon Islands]] |region=[[Tikopia]] |speakers={{sigfig|3320|2}} |date=1999 |ref= |familycolor=Austronesian |fam2=[[Malayo-Polynesian languages|Malayo-Polynesian]] |fam3=[[Oceanic languages|Oceanic]] |fam4=[[Polynesian languages|Polynesian]] |fam5=Ellicean–Eastern |iso3=tkp |glotto=tiko1237 |glottorefname=Tikopia }} The '''Tikopia''' language, or '''Fakatikopia''', is a [[Polynesian outlier|Polynesian Outlier]] language from the island of [[Tikopia]] in the [[Solomon Islands]]. It is closely related to the [[Anuta language]] of the neighboring island of [[Anuta]]; some linguists{{who|date=February 2025}} believe they are dialects of the same language. The language is spoken by approximately 3,320 speakers, and is not considered endangered.[https://www.ethnologue.com/language/tkp/ Tikopia] at [[Ethnologue]] (18th ed., 2015). Tikopia was thorough described by anthropologist [[Raymond Firth]] (1901-2002). == History == Because of its remote and isolated location, Tikopia had little contact with outsiders until well into the twentieth century. One exception is the Melanesian population of [[Vanikoro]], with whom Tikopia islanders have been in regular contact for several centuries.{{sfn|Dillon|1830}}{{sfn|Firth|1961|p=158}} Tikopians occasionally visited other islands, but these trips were limited by the large distances and great hazards involved in making the journey using canoes. Contact with Westerners began sporadically around the beginning of the nineteenth century; in 1927, when Raymond Firth did his initial fieldwork in Tikopia, the indigenous culture was largely intact. The major groups to contact Tikopians were missionaries and labor recruiters. By the 1950s, all the Tikopians had become Christianized, and most of the native ritual practices had ceased. Much of the Tikopian life style has remained intact, although Westernization has occurred.{{cite web |url=http://lucy.ukc.ac.uk/ethnoatlas/hmar/cult_dir/culture.7873 |title=Society-TIKOPIA |last1=Lagace |first1=Robert O. |last2=Swanson |first2=Eleanor C. |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303192132/http://lucy.ukc.ac.uk/ethnoatlas/hmar/cult_dir/culture.7873 |archive-date=3 March 2016}} Nowadays, besides the population living on Tikopia island, the language is also spoken by the Polynesian minority on [[Vanikoro]], who migrated from Tikopia several centuries ago. It is also practised by resettled outlying communities across the Solomon Islands following re-settlement schemes of the 1950's-1960's, like in the communities of Nukufero on [[Pavuvu]], as well as in Nukukaisi on [[Makira island]] though to a lesser extent than Nukufero.{{cite web |date=2020 |title=Tikopia and Santa Ana Resettlement Scheme |url=https://www.solomonencyclopaedia.net/biogs/E000311b.htm |website= |location= |publisher=Solomon Islands Historical Encyclopaedia 1893-1978 |access-date=16 April 2026}}. ==Phonology== ===Consonants=== Tikopia has eleven [[consonant]] [[phonemes]]. They are written {{grapheme|f, k, l, m, n, p, r, s, t, v, w, ng}}.{{cite book |last1=Firth |first1=Raymond |title=Tikopia-English Dictionary |publisher=University of Auckland Press |year=1985 |location=Auckland |page=}} {| class="wikitable" style="text-align: center" |+Consonants{{sfn|Dodenhoff|1982|p=157}} ! ![[Labial consonant|Labial]] ![[Dental consonant|Dental]]/
[[Alveolar consonant|Alveolar]] ![[Velar consonant|Velar]] |- ![[Nasal consonant|Nasal]] |{{IPA link|m}} |{{IPA link|n}} |{{IPA link|ŋ}} |- ![[Plosive]] |{{IPA link|p}} |{{IPA link|t̪}} |{{IPA link|k}} |- ![[Fricative]] |{{IPA link|f}} {{IPA link|v}} |{{IPA link|s}} | |- ![[Trill consonant|Trill]] | |{{IPA link|r}} | |- ![[Lateral consonant|Lateral]] | |{{IPA link|l̪}} | |} * {{IPA|/p, t̪, k/}} are aspirated ({{IPAblink|pʰ}}, {{IPAblink|t̪ʰ}}, {{IPAblink|kʰ}}) before {{IPAslink|u}}.{{sfn|Dodenhoff|1982|p=158}} * {{IPAslink|v}} is {{IPAblink|w}} medially before {{IPAslink|u}}.{{sfn|Dodenhoff|1982|p=159}} It is debated whether or not Tikopia uses {{angbr|l}} or {{angbr|r}}. [[Samuel Hoyt Elbert|Samuel Elbert]] claimed /l/ was used but not /r/.{{sfn|Firth|1963|p=49}} Raymond Firth said, "Dumont D'Urville published a small dictionary in 1834 where 235 words were collected."{{sfn|Firth|1963|p=49}} {{angbr|R}} appeared in 50 words while {{angbr|l}} appeared in only 15. The language changed in over a century and modernly more words are used with {{angbr|l}}. [[Raymond Firth]]'s own work shows that both {{angbr|l}} and {{angbr|r}} phonemes are used, but that words with {{angbr|l}} are far less common.{{sfn|Firth|1963|pp=49-50}} ===Vowels=== {|class="wikitable" style="text-align:center" |+Vowels{{sfn|Dodenhoff|1982|p=157-161}} ! !! In 1928 Firth stayed for a year; he revisited in 1952 for five more months and again in 1966. Only one person, Reverend W. J. Durrad in 1910 who stayed for a duration of 2 months, had recorded documents before. Raymond Firth created a dictionary for the Tikopian language.{{Cite book| publisher = Auckland University Press| isbn = 978-0-19-648037-4| last = Firth| first = Raymond| title = Tikopia-English dictionary / Taranga fakatikopia ma taranga fakainglisi| location = Auckland| date = 1985}} Other materials in the language include: a translation of the Bible; a few YouTube videos; some song books. Linguist [[Alexandre François|A. François]] has also made a handful of audio recordings while doing fieldwork with the Tikopian community of [[Vanikoro]].François, Alexandre. 2020.
